content: Infections are responsible for approximately 25% of the 2.8 million neonatal deaths that occur worldwide each year. Over 95% of neonatal deaths related to sepsis take place in lowand middle-income countries. Hand hygiene is a simple, cost-effective, and affordable method to prevent infections in neonates, making it a practical intervention in resource-limited settings. Therefore, implementing proper hand hygiene practices has the potential to significantly reduce the incidence of infections and infection-related neonatal deaths. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various hand hygiene agents in preventing neonatal infections in both community and healthcare facility settings. Searches for relevant studies were conducted in December 2022 across multiple databases and trial registries, without restrictions on date or language. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cross-over trials, and cluster trials involving pregnant women, mothers, caregivers, healthcare workers, and neonates in either community or healthcare settings. The primary outcomes assessed were the incidence of suspected infections (as defined by the authors of the studies) within the first 28 days of life, bacteriologically confirmed infections within the first 28 days, all-cause mortality within the first seven days of life (early neonatal death), and all-cause mortality from the 8th to the 28th day of life (late neonatal death). Standard Cochrane methodological procedures and the GRADE approach were used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. Six studies were included in the review: two RCTs, one cluster-RCT, and three cross-over trials. Three studies involved a total of 3,281 neonates, while the remaining three studies did not specify the number of neonates included. Three studies involved 279 nurses working in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs), though one study did not specify the number of nurses. A cluster-RCT included 103 pregnant women from 10 villages, and another community-based study involved 258 pregnant women. The studies examined the effectiveness of different hand hygiene practices in reducing the incidence of suspected infections within the first 28 days of life. Regarding the risk of bias, three studies were rated as having a low risk of allocation bias, two as unclear, and one as high risk. For allocation concealment, one study was rated as low risk, one as unclear, and four as high risk. Two studies were rated as having low risk for performance bias, and two as having low risk for attrition bias. When comparing 2% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) to alcohol-based hand sanitiser (61% alcohol with emollients), no study assessed the effect of these agents on the incidence of suspected infections within the first 28 days of life. However, 2% CHG likely reduces the risk of bacteriologically confirmed infections compared to alcohol-based hand sanitiser (relative risk [RR] 0.79, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66 to 0.93; 2,932 participants, 1 study; moderate-certainty evidence). The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 385. Adverse effects on nurses’ skin were reported as mean self-reported and observer-reported skin changes. There may be little to no difference between 2% CHG and alcohol-based hand sanitiser in terms of skin changes, based on very low-certainty evidence (mean difference [MD] -0.80, 95% CI -1.59 to 0.01 for self-reported changes; MD -0.19, 95% CI -0.35 to -0.03 for observer-reported changes; 119 participants, 1 study). No studies reported on all-cause mortality or hospital stay duration for this comparison. When comparing CHG to a combination of plain liquid soap and hand sanitiser, no studies reported on the primary or secondary outcomes except for adverse events. The evidence is very uncertain regarding whether plain soap plus hand sanitiser is better than CHG for nurses’ skin, based on very low-certainty evidence (MD -1.87, 95% CI -3.74 to -0.00; 16 participants, 1 study). When comparing alcohol-based handrub (hand sanitiser) to usual care, the evidence is very uncertain regarding its effectiveness in preventing suspected infections, as reported by mothers (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.39; 103 participants, 1 study; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the evidence is very uncertain regarding its effectiveness in reducing early neonatal mortality (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.00; 103 participants, 1 study; very low-certainty evidence) or late neonatal mortality (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.00; 103 participants, 1 study; very low-certainty evidence). No studies reported on other outcomes for this comparison. In conclusion, there is insufficient data to draw meaningful conclusions about the superiority of one hand hygiene agent over another for preventing neonatal infections. The available evidence is limited and ranges from moderate to very low certainty. As a result, it remains unclear whether any specific hand hygiene agent is more effective than others in reducing neonatal infections or related outcomes.
